title: Robots.txt Explained: What to Block and What to Leave Alone
excerpt: How robots.txt really works: the syntax you need, safe examples for WordPress and shops, the mistakes that wipe out traffic, and how to test the file before launch.
meta_title: Robots.txt Guide: Syntax, Examples and Mistakes
meta_description: Learn how robots.txt works, see safe disallow examples, avoid the mistakes that block a whole site, and test your file before it costs you traffic.
key_takeaways: Robots.txt controls which URLs crawlers may request, not which pages appear in Google.
A disallowed page can still be indexed if other pages link to it, just without a description.
Rules are case-sensitive prefix matches, and the most specific matching rule wins.
Never block the CSS and JavaScript files Google needs to render your pages.
Test every change with Search Console and a crawl before and after the rule takes effect.
content_html:
A new site goes live, everything looks perfect, and a few weeks later organic traffic is close to zero. Someone finally opens the robots.txt file and finds two lines left over from the staging server: User-agent: * and Disallow: /. Every crawler that respects the file has been told to stay away from the whole site.

That is the dramatic version. The everyday version is quieter: a rule that blocks the folder holding your CSS, or a pattern that matches far more URLs than anyone intended.

This guide explains how robots.txt works, the syntax you actually need, safe examples for common setups, the mistakes that cost the most traffic, and how to test the file before it hurts you. It is one step in a wider technical SEO audit checklist, and probably the quickest one to check.

What robots.txt does, and what it does not

Robots.txt is a plain text file at the root of your site that tells crawlers which URLs they may request. It controls crawling, not indexing. That difference causes most of the confusion around it.

Google's introduction to robots.txt says the file is mainly for managing crawler traffic and is not a mechanism for keeping a page out of Google. A disallowed URL can still be indexed if other pages link to it. It just shows up without a description, because Google never read the page.

So if your goal is "keep this page out of search results", robots.txt is the wrong tool. Use a noindex directive or password protection instead. One catch: Google can only see a noindex on a page it is allowed to crawl, so do not block the same URL in robots.txt.

Robots.txt is also voluntary. Well-behaved crawlers like Googlebot and Bingbot follow it. Scrapers and bad bots can ignore it completely.

Where the file lives

The file must sit at the top level of the host, for example https://example.com/robots.txt. A file in a subfolder is ignored.

Each host and protocol gets its own file. According to Google's robots.txt specification notes, a file at https://example.com/robots.txt does not apply to https://shop.example.com/ or to http://example.com/. If you run a blog on a subdomain, it needs its own robots.txt.

The same page also documents a size limit: Google reads up to 500 KiB of the file and ignores anything after that. A small site will never get close, but auto-generated files with thousands of lines can.

Robots.txt syntax in plain English

The file is made of groups. Each group starts with one or more User-agent lines naming the crawler, followed by rules for that crawler. Google supports four fields:

  • User-agent: which crawler the group applies to. * means any crawler that has no more specific group.
  • Disallow: a path the crawler should not request.
  • Allow: a path it may request, used to make exceptions inside a disallowed folder.
  • Sitemap: the full URL of your XML sitemap. This line is independent of the groups and can go anywhere.

Here is a simple, annotated example:

# Rules for every crawler
User-agent: *
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /search
Allow: /search/help

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

A few rules of the format trip people up:

  • Rules are prefix matches. Disallow: /search blocks /search, /search?q=cake and also /searching-for-venues. Add a trailing slash if you only mean the folder.
  • Paths are case-sensitive. Disallow: /Private/ does not block /private/.
  • Wildcards are limited. * matches any sequence of characters and $ marks the end of the URL. So Disallow: /*.pdf$ blocks URLs ending in .pdf.
  • The most specific rule wins. When an allow and a disallow both match, Google uses the one with the longer path. If they are equally specific, it uses the less restrictive one.
  • A crawler follows only one group. If you add a User-agent: Googlebot group, Googlebot ignores the * group entirely, so repeat any shared rules inside it.
  • Some fields are ignored. Google does not support crawl-delay, even though some other search engines do.

The underlying protocol is standardized as RFC 9309, the Robots Exclusion Protocol, though individual search engines can differ on details such as crawl-delay.

Safe robots.txt examples for common setups

For most small sites, the safest robots.txt is a short one. Start from the examples below and only add rules you can explain.

Allow everything (a good default)

User-agent: *
Disallow:

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

An empty Disallow blocks nothing. If your site is a brochure site or a blog with no private areas, this is all you need.

WordPress

WordPress serves a virtual robots.txt by default that blocks /wp-admin/ and allows /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php, because some themes and plugins load front-end content through that file. That default is sensible. Do not add rules for /wp-content/ or /wp-includes/, since those folders hold the CSS, JavaScript and images your pages need to render.

Online shops

Shops often generate thousands of near-identical URLs from internal search, filters and sorting. Blocking those can save crawling for your real product and category pages:

  • Disallow: /cart/ and Disallow: /checkout/ for pages with no search value.
  • Disallow: /search for internal search results.
  • Disallow: /*?sort= for sorted duplicates of the same category.

Before blocking a parameter, check that none of your canonical URLs use it. If ?page=2 is how products deep in a category get discovered, blocking it hides those products from crawlers.

Hosted platforms

On hosted builders, you may not be able to edit robots.txt directly. The platform manages it, usually through a "hide from search engines" setting. Check that setting is off once the site launches.

The robots.txt mistakes that cost the most traffic

These are the problems worth checking every time you audit a site, roughly in order of damage.

  1. Staging rules left in place. Disallow: / under User-agent: * blocks the entire site. Add "check robots.txt" to your launch checklist and look again after every deployment that touches server config.
  2. Blocking CSS and JavaScript. Google renders pages much like a browser does. Google's intro to robots.txt warns that if missing resources make a page harder to understand, you should not block them. A page that renders as unstyled text, or as an empty shell when the content is loaded by JavaScript, is judged on what Google can see.
  3. Using disallow to remove a page. As covered above, a blocked page can stay in the index. Worse, if the page has a noindex tag, the block stops Google from ever reading it.
  4. Blocking pages that carry redirects or canonicals. If an old URL redirects to a new one but robots.txt blocks the old URL, crawlers never see the redirect.
  5. Listing secret paths. Robots.txt is public. Anyone can read it, so a line like Disallow: /new-pricing-draft/ advertises the very page you wanted to hide. Protect private content with a login.
  6. Overly broad patterns. Disallow: /p meant for /p/ also blocks /products/ and /pricing. Always test patterns against real URLs.
  7. A robots.txt that errors. If the file returns a server error, Google's documentation says it stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours while it retries. A 404 for robots.txt, by contrast, is treated as "no restrictions".

How to test your robots.txt

Never publish a robots.txt change without testing it against real URLs. Three checks cover most cases:

  1. Read the live file. Open /robots.txt in a private browser window and confirm it is the version you expect, returns a 200 and is plain text.
  2. Use Search Console. Google's guide to creating and testing a robots.txt file points to the robots.txt report in Search Console, which shows the version Google last fetched and any parsing problems. For a specific page, the URL Inspection tool tells you whether it is blocked.
  3. Crawl your site both ways. Run one crawl that respects robots.txt and one that ignores it, then compare. Any important URL that appears only in the second crawl is blocked. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO has optional robots.txt compliance, which makes this comparison easy.

Say you run a small events site and want to block internal search. You add Disallow: /search, then crawl with robots.txt respected. If your "Searching for a venue? Read this" guide at /searching-for-a-venue has vanished from the results, your rule is too broad. Change it to Disallow: /search/ or Disallow: /search? to match how your search URLs are actually built.

Robots.txt and your sitemap

The Sitemap: line is the one part of robots.txt that helps crawlers find more, not less. Listing your sitemap there means any search engine that reads robots.txt can discover it, not only the ones where you submitted it by hand.

Keep the two files consistent. If a URL is in your sitemap, it should not be blocked in robots.txt. That contradiction tells Google you both want and do not want the page crawled. Learn how to build a clean XML sitemap that only lists pages worth indexing.

If you are still getting to grips with crawling and indexing in general, our plain-English intro to SEO basics explains how the pieces fit together.

The bottom line

Robots.txt is a small file with a big blast radius. It tells crawlers where not to go, but it does not remove pages from Google, and it cannot hide anything, because anyone can read it.

For most small sites, the best robots.txt is short: block genuinely useless crawl paths like carts and internal search, never block CSS or JavaScript, list your sitemap, and test every change against real URLs.

Your next step: open yoursite.com/robots.txt right now, check every Disallow line against a real URL, and confirm nothing important is blocked.

faqs.question: Does every website need a robots.txt file?
faqs.answer: No. If there is no robots.txt file, crawlers assume they can crawl everything, which is fine for many small sites. A short file is still useful because it can list your sitemap location.

faqs.question: How do I block Google from a page completely?
faqs.answer: Do not rely on robots.txt for that. Add a noindex meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header and make sure the page is crawlable so Google can see it, or put the content behind a login.

faqs.question: How long does it take Google to notice a robots.txt change?
faqs.answer: Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours, so a change usually takes effect within a day. If you need Google to pick up an urgent change sooner, Google documents how to submit an updated robots.txt file through Search Console.

faqs.question: Can I block AI crawlers with robots.txt?
faqs.answer: You can add groups for specific user agents that a crawler operator documents, and crawlers that respect robots.txt will follow them. Check each operator's own documentation for the exact user-agent name, and remember that robots.txt is voluntary.
